title: CS Quest 2.1 · Bug hunt (Test and debug)
name: Bug hunt (Test and debug)
summary: Students test one program against three test boards and fix it without breaking the others. In the Debug Lab every level starts with a broken program and three tabs that show a check mark or an X per test after each run; level 6 is an edge case, an odd board that breaks a hidden assumption about the gems, and level 7 adds the rule never bump. Fewest edits earn the most stars. One device per student.
iCan: test one program against several test boards and read the results
find the input that breaks a program, including the odd one out
fix a bug without breaking the tests that already passed
materials: Bug Cards printable (printed programs with three test boards each, a test table, fix stickers)
doNow: Find the mistake in each one: 2 + 2 = 5. Teh cat sat on the mat. A route that says turn left when the flag is on the right. Then write one test you would run to prove each fix.
plan: Explore: one program, three test boards, one fix

warmup.why: first lesson of the unit: the unit opener, the vocabulary item and today's three exit items as a pre-test; nobody is expected to know them yet, so say so

do: Open Robo Route at Debug Lab on the projector (Open game at this chapter). Level 1 already has a program and three tabs above the board: three test boards. Press Run and read the tabs out loud: a check mark for a test that passes, an X for one that fails. Open a failing test and press Step until Bolt turns the wrong way at the corner.

Change only that block: turn right becomes turn left in the else part. Run again and watch all three tabs turn to check marks. Point at the edits counter: one edit, three stars. Then describe level 6 in one sentence: tests 1 and 2 pass, test 3 has a different number of gems, and the program assumed every board had the same gems before the goal.
say: Programs break. Good programmers expect it and test on purpose. A test case is one board with a known right answer; one board can hide a bug, three boards catch it.
An edge case is the odd input, like a maze with no gems or a hallway two squares longer. It breaks the assumption you did not know you had made. A fix is finished only when every test passes again.
ask: Which test board caught the bug, and why did we need more than one?
explore.afterAsk: Write a test table on the board with three rows: test, expected, actual, pass? Fill it for level 1 before and after the fix. Leave it up for Play.
explore.bigIdea: Test a program against several boards, find the one that fails, fix the smallest thing, and run every test again.

play.stretch: the chapter, then 3 stars: the fewest edits on every level; level 6 is the edge case, level 7 says never bump
play.solo: one device per student; every level has three test boards; a neighbor may read your program and the tabs out loud, never touch your screen
lookFors: fixing for test 1 and never running tests 2 and 3, then moving on with an X still showing
deleting the whole program instead of stepping through the failing test
adding blocks around the bug instead of changing the wrong one: the edits counter goes up and the stars go down
play.misconception: A program that passes one test is not finished: a fix must pass every test board, including the odd one, and the tests run again after every change.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: Which test board caught your bug on level 4, and what would have happened with only one board?
Level 6: tests 1 and 2 passed and test 3 did not. What hidden assumption about the gems did the program make, and how did the fix remove it?
showMe: One student shows level 6 on the projector: the three tabs before the fix, the step-through of test 3, and the tabs after.

exit.sentencePrompt: Pick one bug you fixed today. Which test caught it, what did you expect and what did Bolt do, what did you change, and what did you run afterward?
exit.frame: Test ___ caught it: I expected ___ but Bolt ___, so I changed ___. Then I ran ___ again.

rubric.line: Systematic testing: the test, expected vs actual, the fix
levels: Names a bug or a fix with no test behind it
Names the test that caught the bug, what was expected and what happened, and the change made
Also says every test was run again after the fix, or names the edge case and the assumption it broke

exit.paper: exit half-sheet (two per page) with the three items and the sentence frame

support: hint 1 names the failing test; step mode on that board shows the first wrong block
the test table from Explore stays on the board; read-aloud on
every level has exactly one bug; the fix takes one to four edits
stretch: 3 stars on every level: the fewest edits
level 7: never bump on any board, then explain why the when block alone was not enough
design one more test board that would break a neighbor's fix, and say which assumption it attacks

unpluggedTwin.title: Bug Cards, three tests
materials: printed programs with three small test boards each
a test table per pair (test, expected, actual, pass?)
steps: Each pair gets a bug card: one program and three boards. One partner runs the token through board 1 line by line while the other fills in the test table row: expected, actual, pass or fail. Then boards 2 and 3.
Find the board that fails and the first line where expected and actual split apart. Fix only that line with a sticker.
Run all three boards again from the top. A fix that breaks a board that used to pass is not a fix. Count the stickers: fewest wins.

Edge case round: each pair draws a fourth board meant to break another pair's program (no gems, a longer hallway, the flag right before a wall) and swaps. Share: which assumption did your board attack?

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: find the mistake in 2 + 2 = 5, in Teh cat sat on the mat, and in a route that says turn left when the flag is on the right, then write one test that would prove each fix.

Play Robo Route, chapter Debug Lab (Pro), one device each, for 20 minutes. Classes, then the lesson, then Play. If the game asks, the quest code is 6 2 1 0. Goal: 4 levels. No warm-up and no projector needed; playing signed out is fine.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it.

shortPeriod40.discuss: Which test board caught your bug on level 4, and what would have happened with only one board?
shortPeriod40.keep: the exit ticket is never cut; in 5 minutes of Explore fix level 1 and only describe level 6

add: the Bug Cards, three tests twin (15 minutes) before Play
the fewest-edits stretch and level 7 after Play
Best Route, the next chapter, for 10 minutes (quest code 7 2 0 0 from the game's own menu): build the flowchart first, then a program that must match it on every test board

notes: Stars count edits: the fewest edits from the starter program earn three stars, so deleting everything is the slow and starless path.
The warm-up is a pre-test for unit 2: nobody is expected to know the answers yet. Say so before you start.
Best Route at this band is the flowchart chapter: the program is checked against a chart the student builds first. It is the stretch here and the twin of the planning id from 1.1.
Vocabulary beyond the five on the learn card: debug, step mode, assumption.
Debug mode works signed out, so the sub plan needs no login. One device per student at this band.
